timeline_list.title: The Comeback
timeline_list.description: Zhi qu wei hu shan (Taking Tiger Mountain by Strategy, 1970) is the first Chinese film to be released since the start of the Cultural Revolution.

timeline_list.title: Vietnam at the Berlin Film Festival
timeline_list.description: The Berlin Film Festival collapses over O.K. (1970), a film by Michael Verhoeven (b. 1938) that offers a controversial depiction of American atrocities in the Vietnam War.

timeline_list.title: A Good Start
timeline_list.description: Med Hondo's (b. 1936) debut with Soleil O (1973) makes waves and opens the new decade for African cinema in striking fashion.

timeline_list.title: The Kung Fu Explosion
timeline_list.description: The Chinese Boxer (1970) hits theaters, and with it comes the kung fu film explosion.

timeline_list.title: Do you feel lucky, punk?
timeline_list.description: Dirty Harry (1971) hits theaters the same year that Charles Manson and his co-defendants are found guilty on all charges.

timeline_list.title: Blaxploitation
timeline_list.description: Shaft (1971) and Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song (1971) are released, marking the beginning of Blaxploitation (also called Blacksploitation).

timeline_list.title: The Foundations of Conspiracy Thrillers
timeline_list.description: Alan J. Pakula (1928-1998) begins his "paranoia trilogy" with Klute (1971). The film establishes the themes that became essential to conspiracy thrillers.

timeline_list.title: A Clockwork Orange
timeline_list.description: Directed by Stanley Kubrick (1928-1999), A Clockwork Orange (1971) raises questions about individual thought, personal choice and violence.

timeline_list.title: Electronic surveillance
timeline_list.description: Directed by Sidney Lumet (b. 1924), The Anderson Tapes (1971) introduces electronic surveillance as a major theme.

timeline_list.title: The Revival of Mob Movies
timeline_list.description: The Godfather (1972) is released, becoming a tremendous success and a cultural symbol. More than that, the film turns out to be one of the driving forces behind the revival of mob movies from the 1970s through the 1990s.

timeline_list.title: Sex, Butter and Brando
timeline_list.description: Ultimo tango a Parigi (Last Tango in Paris, 1972) generates more international headlines than any previous non-English-language film. The film becomes one of the most prominent symbols of sexual violence in cinema.

timeline_list.title: Pornography in Vogue
timeline_list.description: Deep Throat briefly makes pornography fashionable and becomes highly profitable.

timeline_list.title: Master of Disaster
timeline_list.description: Irwin Allen (1916-1991) produces and co-directs The Poseidon Adventure (1972), becoming the "master of disaster" of the 1970s.

timeline_list.title: Hysteria and Fear
timeline_list.description: The Exorcist (1973) is released, causing hysteria in the US. Reports of people feeling sick and having seizures make the front pages of the major newspapers of the time. The film marks the beginning of a new era of religious-themed horror films, such as The Omen (1976).

timeline_list.title: Bruce Lee
timeline_list.description: Enter the Dragon (1973) hits theaters, propelling Bruce Lee (1940-1973) to stardom and becoming a cultural landmark and the foundation for the kung fu films released ever since.

timeline_list.title: The Beginning of Slasher Films
timeline_list.description: The first of the slasher movies, Black Christmas (1974) features shots from the killer's point of view. Tobe Hooper (1943-2017) perfects the formula with The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974).

timeline_list.title: Conspiracy and Distrust
timeline_list.description: Nixon resigns the presidency. The Conversation (1974) and The Parallax View (1974) explore themes such as conspiracy and distrust.

timeline_list.title: Neo-noir
timeline_list.description: Roman Polanski (b. 1933) releases Chinatown (1974), one of the greatest symbols of neo-noir (new film noir).

timeline_list.title: Theo Angelopoulos
timeline_list.description: Theo Angelopoulos's (b. 1935) third film, O Thiasos (The Travelling Players, 1975), confirms the emergence of an exceptional new talent in Greece, with a remarkable personal style.

timeline_list.title: Blockbusters
timeline_list.description: Jaws (1975) is released in the summer, surpassing the box office of The Godfather (1972). It becomes the first "event movie", setting the standard for blockbuster films ever since.

timeline_list.title: Women in African Cinema
timeline_list.description: Safi Faye (b. 1943) becomes the first female director from sub-Saharan Africa with the feature film Kaddu Beykat (Letter from My Village, 1975).

timeline_list.title: The Rocky Horror Picture Show
timeline_list.description: The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975) becomes a cult film, earning the title of longest-running film, screened at the same theater in Munich, Germany, every week for more than 27 years.

timeline_list.title: VHS
timeline_list.description: Video recorders spread in the Betamax and (a year later) VHS formats, allowing people to record films and watch them at home.

timeline_list.title: Teenage Heroines and Superpowers
timeline_list.description: Carrie (1976) launches the wave of teenage heroines, protagonists with psychic or telekinetic powers, and adaptations of horror novels by writer Stephen King.

timeline_list.title: Government Scandals
timeline_list.description: Taxi Driver (1976) and All the President's Men (1976) reflect the psychological scars of the Vietnam War and the Watergate scandal, respectively.

timeline_list.title: May the Force Be with You!
timeline_list.description: Star Wars (1977) is released, a landmark in popular culture. More than that, its success reveals audiences' appetite for simpler mainstream cinema.

timeline_list.title: Disco to the Sound of the Bee Gees
timeline_list.description: Saturday Night Fever (1977) and disco take the world by storm. The album of songs from the film became the best-selling soundtrack of all time.

timeline_list.title: Psychopathic Killers
timeline_list.description: Halloween (1978) draws on Psycho (1960) and on the giallo films of Mario Bava (1914-1980) and Dario Argento (b. 1940) to cement the formula of the psycho-killer film.

timeline_list.title: Jackie Chan
timeline_list.description: Zui quan (Drunken Master, 1978) becomes a hit, presenting kung fu blended with physical comedy, something that became a hallmark of Jackie Chan's (b. 1954) career.

timeline_list.title: Is It a Bird? Is It a Plane?
timeline_list.description: Superman (1978) hits theaters, giving birth to the superhero film.

timeline_list.title: I love the smell of napalm in the morning
timeline_list.description: Apocalypse Now (1979) is released after a troubled production. The film wins the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival and is nominated for the Oscar for Best Picture.

timeline_list.title: Horror and Monsters
timeline_list.description: Alien (1979), released four years after Jaws (1975), breathes new life into monster movies.

timeline_list.title: Mad Max
timeline_list.description: George Miller (b. 1945) directs Mad Max (1979). The film becomes the most profitable movie of all time relative to its cost and introduces Mel Gibson (b. 1956) to the world.

timeline_list.title: Chuck Norris
timeline_list.description: Former karate champion Chuck Norris stars in the martial arts film A Force of One (1979).

timeline_list.title: Friday the 13th
timeline_list.description: Friday the 13th (1980) is released, kicking off an even bigger wave of slasher films in the 1980s.

timeline_list.title: ZAZ
timeline_list.description: The parody Airplane! (1980) earns Golden Globe and BAFTA nominations. The film marks the start of a wave of parody films using the ZAZ formula in the 1980s. These comedies inspired the Scary Movie series.

timeline_list.title: E.T. Phone Home
timeline_list.description: Despite its modest scale, E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982) breaks box office records and becomes the most successful film of all time.

timeline_list.title: Monty Python
timeline_list.description: Time Bandits (1981) builds on the success of the Monty Python films and taps into the growing demand for fantasy comedies for audiences of all ages.

timeline_list.title: Jerry Bruckheimer and Don Simpson
timeline_list.description: The success of Flashdance (1983) marks the beginning of Jerry Bruckheimer and Don Simpson's dominance over the production of mass-market Hollywood films.

timeline_list.title: Steve Martin
timeline_list.description: Steve Martin co-writes and stars in The Man with Two Brains (1983), confirming his position as one of the great working comedians.

timeline_list.title: Mockumentary
timeline_list.description: This Is Spinal Tap (1984) is released, a comedy hit about a fictional British heavy metal band that gave rise to the mockumentary genre.

timeline_list.title: I'll be back
timeline_list.description: Arnold Schwarzenegger (b. 1947) plays a killer robot from the future in the first film of the Terminator series (The Terminator, 1984). The film is considered a landmark of science fiction cinema.

timeline_list.title: Sundance Film Festival
timeline_list.description: The Sundance Institute holds its first film festival in Utah, in the US, to promote independent cinema from around the world.

timeline_list.title: Back to the Future
timeline_list.description: Back to the Future (1985) defines the blockbuster of the Reagan era.

timeline_list.title: Teen Comedies
timeline_list.description: Teen comedies rake in box office money with Back to the Future (1985), The Breakfast Club (1985), The Goonies (1985) and Weird Science (1985).

timeline_list.title: Life moves pretty fast...
timeline_list.description: Ferris Bueller's Day Off (1986) keeps the teen wave going in theaters, establishing John Hughes (1950-2009) as one of the great directors of the 1980s.

timeline_list.title: Studio Ghibli
timeline_list.description: Studio Ghibli officially releases its first film, Hauru no Ugoku Shiro (Howl's Moving Castle, 2004), following the success of Kaze no Tani no Naushika (Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind, 1984).

timeline_list.title: Dirty Dancing
timeline_list.description: Dirty Dancing (1987) becomes one of the most iconic films of the 1980s.

timeline_list.title: Good morning, Vietnam! Hey, this is not a test
timeline_list.description: Barry Levinson (b. 1942) directs Good Morning, Vietnam (1987), based on the work of an armed forces radio DJ who became popular among the troops serving in Vietnam.

timeline_list.title: Die Hard!
timeline_list.description: Bruce Willis (b. 1955) wears torn clothes to play cop John McClane in Die Hard (1988).

timeline_list.title: Bumping the lamp
timeline_list.description: Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988) hits theaters, dazzling audiences with the way its cartoons are integrated into live-action scenes. And for the first time, we see Mickey Mouse and Bugs Bunny in the same scene.

timeline_list.title: Tim Burton's Batman
timeline_list.description: Batman (1989) updates the superhero blockbuster - and becomes the first film to gross 100 million dollars in its first 10 days of release.

timeline_list.title: Independent Cinema
timeline_list.description: Indie cinema comes of age with sex, lies, and videotape (1989), a hit that paves the way for director Steven Soderbergh (b. 1963) and the Miramax studio.

timeline_list.title: Do the Right Thing
timeline_list.description: Do the Right Thing (1989), by Spike Lee (b. 1957), hits theaters, establishing the director as one of the great breakthroughs of the era. The film was a forerunner of films focused on marginalized urban neighborhoods and African American characters.
